name: The Eight Region Strings Stored In District A3
description: district.A3 stores the region as one of exactly eight strings: 'Prague', 'central Bohemia', 'east Bohemia', 'north Bohemia', 'south Bohemia', 'west Bohemia', 'north Moravia' and 'south Moravia'. Note that the country is not all Bohemia — two of the eight regions are Moravia, so a question about north or south Moravia matches a real value and must not be bent onto a Bohemia one. Match with exact equality and keep the case exactly as stored: the compass word is lower case and the region name is capitalised, so it is 'south Bohemia' and never 'South Bohemia', while 'Prague' stands alone as a capitalised single word. Related phrasings: north Bohemia, east Bohemia, south Moravia, region A3, crimes by region.
sql: SELECT A3, A16 FROM district WHERE A3 IN ('north Bohemia', 'east Bohemia')

name: ISO Date Strings In Trans Date And The Account And Loan Dates
description: trans.date and account/loan date columns are ISO 'YYYY-MM-DD' strings (e.g. question 1998/9/2 → '1998-09-02'). Always zero-pad month and day. Related phrasings: transaction date, ISO date, YYYY-MM-DD.
sql: SELECT trans_id, account_id, amount, date FROM trans WHERE date = '1998-09-02' AND amount = 5100

name: Home District Of A Client And Branch District Of An Account
description: client.district_id is where the person lives and account.district_id is the branch where the account was opened. They disagree for a substantial minority of client-account pairs, so the two paths return different sets of people and the choice changes the answer. Let the subject of the question pick the path. When the question is about people — how many clients or customers there are, their gender, whether they are men or women, when they were born, what proportion of them are women — join client straight to district on client.district_id and do not travel through disp and account. That holds even when the wording mentions an account or sounds like a branch, as with how many clients who opened their accounts in a named branch were women, or the gender of the oldest client who opened an account in the district with the highest average salary: the client is the subject, so the client's own district decides it, and bringing in disp and account both lengthens the path and changes the answer. When the subject is the account, the loan, the transaction or the standing order, join account to district on account.district_id instead. This settles which district column describes a person; it does not govern a question that asks for the account numbers belonging to such clients, where the account is the answer and carries a district of its own. Related phrasings: clients in a district, average salary district, account holders in a region, opened an account in, clients at a branch.
sql: SELECT T1.client_id, T1.birth_date FROM client AS T1 INNER JOIN district AS T2 ON T1.district_id = T2.district_id WHERE T2.A2 = 'Jesenik'

name: What The Coded District Columns A2 A4 A11 A12 A13 A15 And A16 Mean
description: The district table codes its columns behind letter-and-number names. A2 is the district name and A3 the wider region. A4 is the number of inhabitants and is stored as text, so it sorts lexically unless it is cast to an integer. A11 is the average salary. A12 and A13 are the unemployment rates for 1995 and 1996, and A15 and A16 are the numbers of committed crimes for those same two years. A question naming a year picks the matching column of the pair, so the unemployment rate in 1996 is A13 while the 1995 one is A12, and the crimes committed in 1996 are A16 against A15 for 1995. Related phrasings: unemployment rate, crime rate, number of inhabitants, average salary, district name, region.
sql: SELECT A2, A12, A13 FROM district WHERE A13 > A12

name: District Id As A Branch Location Against A2 As A Name And A3 As A Region
description: A district is identified by district.district_id, and that identifier is what names the location of a branch. When a question asks for a branch location, or asks which district something happened in and wants the district itself rather than a description of it, project district_id. A2 holds the district name, so a question asking for the district name projects A2, and a question asking for the branch location together with the district name projects district_id and A2 side by side. A3 is the wider region such as Prague or south Bohemia; it answers a question about the region and is not a location or a name, so it does not stand in for either. Related phrasings: branch location, list their location, which district, district name, name the district.
sql: SELECT T2.district_id, T2.A2 FROM account AS T1 INNER JOIN district AS T2 ON T1.district_id = T2.district_id WHERE T1.account_id = 1234

name: Trans Id Client Id And Account Id As The Answer To A Listing
description: A request to list transactions, clients or accounts asks for the identifying column of that thing and nothing else: trans_id for a transaction, client_id for a client, account_id for an account. Return that single column rather than every column of the table, and keep doing so when the question adds a filter such as the district an account belongs to, the kind of transaction, or a date range, because a filter narrows the rows without widening the projection. Other columns join the projection only where the question names them, as when it asks for the id and the district together. Related phrasings: list all the transactions, please list, list out the accounts, name the clients, provide the ids.
sql: SELECT T1.trans_id FROM trans AS T1 WHERE T1.operation = 'VYBER' AND T1.amount > 5000

name: Repeated Account Rows When Trans Disp Or Loan Joins An Account
description: How many accounts, clients or transactions there are is answered by a plain COUNT over the joined rows. A join to trans, disp or loan repeats the account once per movement, disposition or loan, and that repetition is kept rather than removed, so the count runs over the rows the join produces and not over the separate things behind them. Counting how many accounts in a region made a transaction with a given partner bank therefore counts the qualifying rows, and wrapping the key in DISTINCT collapses them and returns a far smaller number than intended. DISTINCT belongs to a count only where the question asks how many different values of something there are, such as how many districts clients come from, since there the repeated value is itself what is being counted. Related phrasings: how many accounts, how many clients, count the transactions, number of accounts in a region.
sql: SELECT COUNT(T2.account_id) FROM trans AS T1 INNER JOIN account AS T2 ON T1.account_id = T2.account_id WHERE T1.operation = 'VYBER KARTOU'

name: A District Name Beside Its Count And A Client Id Beside Its Account Id
description: A question that names several things expects a column for each of them, in the order it names them. Asking for the districts and the number of female clients in each returns the district beside that count, not the district alone; asking for a list of clients and the branch their account belongs to returns the client and the account together; asking how many owner and how many disponent dispositions there are returns two figures side by side, one conditional sum for each type, rather than a single total covering both. A filter is not a request: a condition that narrows the rows, such as a year or an amount threshold, does not earn a column. The test is whether a reader could answer every part of the question from the rows that come back, and where one part is a measure and another names the thing measured, both belong in the projection. Related phrasings: list the districts and the number of, provide the id and the age, state the district and region, how many owner and disponent.
sql: SELECT T2.A3, COUNT(T1.client_id) FROM client AS T1 INNER JOIN district AS T2 ON T1.district_id = T2.district_id GROUP BY T2.A3

name: Owner And Disponent Rows In Disp Between A Client And An Account
description: disp is the link between a person and an account, carrying client_id, account_id and a type that is either 'OWNER' or 'DISPONENT'. It is needed only where a question joins something about a person to something about an account, such as the gender of a borrower, the birthday of whoever took out a loan, or who owns an account. A question that concerns accounts alone does not need it, and adding it there duplicates every account once per person attached to it and inflates any count. An account reaches its loan directly, because loan carries account_id, so counting the accounts that have a loan or are eligible for one joins account to loan on that key. Being eligible for a loan is not a property an account carries and is not a status to test: it means a row exists for that account in loan, so the join to loan is itself the condition, and leaving the join out counts every account in the district instead of the ones with a loan. The standing orders in order and the movements in trans hang off the account in the same way, while card is the exception: it carries disp_id, so a question about credit cards does travel through disp. Related phrasings: accounts eligible for loans, accounts with a loan, how many accounts, owner of the account, disponent.
sql: SELECT T1.account_id, T2.amount FROM account AS T1 INNER JOIN loan AS T2 ON T1.account_id = T2.account_id WHERE T2.status = 'A'
